text: Leo Strauss (September 20, 1899 – October 18, 1973) was a German-American political philosopher and historian of philosophy whose work profoundly influenced twentieth-century political theory in the United States and the study of classical political thought. He is best known for his interpretations of ancient and medieval philosophy, his account of classical natural right, and his claim that philosophers often wrote esoterically, presenting different teachings to general and specialist audiences. Strauss argued that the modern turn in philosophy, beginning with Niccolò Machiavelli and culminating in historicism and relativism, marked a decisive break with classical understandings of politics and the good life. His work aimed to recover the questions and methods of ancient political philosophy as a corrective to the perceived crisis of modern thought. His scholarship encompassed studies of Plato, Aristotle, Xenophon, Thomas Hobbes, Baruch Spinoza, Friedrich Nietzsche, and the medieval Islamic and Jewish philosophical traditions, particularly Al-Farabi and Maimonides. Central to his writings were the tensions between reason and revelation, the nature of political prudence, and the relationship between philosophy and political authority. His methodological emphasis on close textual reading, the pedagogical value of classical texts, and the critique of modernity formed the basis of what became known as "Straussian" approaches to political theory. Born in Kirchhain, Hesse-Nassau (a province of the Kingdom of Prussia in the German Empire), to Jennie Strauss (née David) and Hugo Strauss, Strauss was raised as an Orthodox Jew, though his family did not fully embrace Orthodox practice. His father and uncle ran a farm supply and livestock business inherited from Meyer (1835–1919), a leading member of the local Jewish community. After attending the Kirchhain Volksschule and the Protestant Rektoratsschule, he studied at the Gymnasium Philippinum in Marburg, graduating in 1917. He served in the German army during World War I from July 5, 1917, to December 1918. He earned his doctorate in 1921 from the University of Hamburg with a thesis on F. H. Jacobi, supervised by Ernst Cassirer, and attended courses at the Universities of Freiburg and Marburg, including those taught by Edmund Husserl and Martin Heidegger. He joined a Jewish fraternity and worked for the German Zionist movement, meeting intellectuals such as Norbert Elias, Leo Löwenthal, Hannah Arendt, and Walter Benjamin, who remained an admirer of his work throughout his life. His closest friend was Jacob Klein, and he engaged intellectually with Gerhard Krüger, Karl Löwith, Julius Guttmann, Hans-Georg Gadamer, Franz Rosenzweig (to whom he dedicated his first book), Gershom Scholem, Alexander Altmann, and Paul Kraus, who married Strauss's sister Bettina; Strauss and his wife later adopted Paul and Bettina Kraus's child after both parents died in the Middle East. He maintained vigorous epistolary exchanges with several of these friends, many of which are published in the Gesammelte Schriften (Collected Writings), some in translation. He also had a discourse with Carl Schmitt, which he discontinued after Schmitt failed to respond to his letters. In 1932, after receiving a Rockefeller Fellowship, Strauss left his position at the Higher Institute for Jewish Studies in Berlin for Paris, where he married Marie (Miriam) Bernsohn, a widow with a young child, whom he had known in Germany. He adopted her son, Thomas, and later his sister's child, Jenny Strauss Clay (who later became a professor of classics at the University of Virginia); he and Miriam had no biological children. At his death, he was survived by Thomas, Jenny Strauss Clay, and three grandchildren. He became a lifelong friend of Alexandre Kojève and was on friendly terms with Raymond Aron and Étienne Gilson. Due to the Nazis' rise to power, he chose not to return to Germany. He found shelter in England, where in 1935 he secured temporary employment at the University of Cambridge with the help of his in-law David Daube. While in England, he became close to R. H. Tawney and had less favorable relations with Isaiah Berlin. Unable to secure permanent employment, he moved to the United States in 1937 under the patronage of Harold Laski, who helped him obtain a brief lectureship. After a short stint as a research fellow at Columbia University, he joined The New School, where he worked in the political science faculty from 1938 to 1948 and took on adjunct roles. In 1939, he served as a visiting professor at Hamilton College. He became a U.S. citizen in 1944 and in 1949 was appointed professor of political science at the University of Chicago, holding the Robert Maynard Hutchins Distinguished Service Professorship until 1969. In 1953, he coined the phrase reductio ad Hitlerum, a play on reductio ad absurdum, suggesting that comparing an argument to one of Hitler's is a fallacy of irrelevance. In 1954, he met Karl Löwith and Hans-Georg Gadamer in Heidelberg and delivered a public speech on Socrates. In 1965, he was offered a temporary lectureship in Hamburg, which he declined due to health reasons, and received an honorary doctorate from the University of Hamburg and the German Order of Merit through the German representative in Chicago. In 1969, he moved to Claremont McKenna College in California for a year and then to St. John's College, Annapolis in 1970, where he was the Scott Buchanan Distinguished Scholar in Residence until his death from pneumonia in 1973. He was buried in the Annapolis Hebrew Cemetery with his wife Miriam Bernsohn Strauss, who died in 1985, and Psalm 114 was read at the funeral service at the request of family and friends. Strauss's thought is characterized by two main themes: the critique of modernity and the recovery of classical political philosophy. He argued that modernity, emerging in 15th-century Italian city states especially through Machiavelli, represented a radical break from Western tradition, leading to nihilism, relativism, historicism, and scientism. He claimed that modern political and social sciences, based on empirical observation and rational analysis, failed to address fundamental questions of human nature, morality, and justice, reducing humans to objects of manipulation. He criticized modern liberalism for lacking moral and spiritual foundations and for undermining religion, tradition, and natural law. To counter modernity's crisis, Strauss advocated a return to classical political philosophy, arguing that ancient and medieval thinkers had a deeper understanding of human nature and society. He promoted careful, respectful reading of classical texts, asserting that their authors wrote esoterically—using layered meanings, irony, paradox, or self-contradiction—to protect themselves and the regime from persecution, to attract the right readers, and to engage in a dialogue across time, which he called "the great conversation." This esoteric writing, he argued, was not about hiding a secret message for a select few versus a public one, but about conveying a deeper, irreducible message at the tacit heart of the text. Influenced by his Jewish background and engagement with Islamic and Jewish medieval philosophy, especially Al-Farabi and Maimonides, Strauss saw these thinkers as models for reconciling reason and revelation, philosophy and theology, Athens and Jerusalem. For Strauss, politics and philosophy were necessarily intertwined; he viewed Socrates' trial as the moment political philosophy began, emphasizing that Socrates argued philosophers must consider human nature—defined by Aristotle as that of a "political animal"—before studying nature. However, he also held that the ends of politics and philosophy were irreconcilable and irreducible. Strauss distinguished "scholars" from "great thinkers," identifying himself as a scholar, noting that most self-described philosophers are actually cautious scholars who reason about the differences between great thinkers, while great thinkers boldly confront major problems. In Natural Right and History (1953), he critiqued Max Weber's epistemology, engaged with the relativism of Martin Heidegger (unnamed), analyzed the evolution of natural rights through Hobbes and Locke, and critiqued Rousseau and Burke, with excerpts from Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero at the heart of the work. Much of his philosophy was a reaction to Heidegger, whom he believed must be understood and confronted before modern political theory could be fully formulated, requiring engagement with ontology and the history of metaphysics. Strauss wrote that Nietzsche was the first philosopher to properly understand historicism, rooted in Hegelian philosophy of history; Heidegger, in Strauss's view, sanitized and politicized Nietzsche, while Nietzsche believed that all principles—including belief in progress—would eventually be shown to be false, and that the only way forward was to "voluntarily choose life-giving delusion instead of deadly truth, that one fabricate a myth." Heidegger believed Nietzsche's nihilism was a "myth" stemming from a defective Western conception of Being traced to Plato. In correspondence with Kojève, Strauss stated that Hegel was correct in asserting that an end of history implies an end to classical political philosophy. In the late 1930s, Strauss first called for a reconsideration of the distinction between exoteric (public) and esoteric (secret) teaching. In 1952, he published Persecution and the Art of Writing, arguing that serious writers use esoteric methods to protect themselves and the regime, attract the right readers, and repel the wrong ones, with the act of uncovering the interior message itself being a form of philosophical reasoning. Drawing on Maimonides and Al-Farabi and referencing Plato's Phaedrus, Strauss proposed that the classical and medieval art of esoteric writing is the proper medium for philosophic learning, as it guides readers to think independently rather than imparting knowledge. He presented Maimonides as a "closet nonbeliever" who obfuscated his message for political reasons. His hermeneutical argument, reiterated in works like The City and Man (1964), is that before the 19th century, Western scholars understood that philosophical writing does not belong in any polity, as it questions conventional wisdom at its roots and must guard against readers who believe themselves authoritative or defenders of the status quo. Philosophers of the past used esoteric communication to avoid persecution, especially from those few whom the many regarded as the most righteous guardians of morality. Strauss explicitly followed Gotthold Ephraim Lessing in arguing that medieval political philosophers, like their ancient counterparts, adapted their language to prevailing moral views to avoid being condemned as heretical or unjust—not by the "many" who did not read, but by the "few" who were seen as moral authorities. Modern social science is flawed, according to Strauss, because it assumes the fact–value distinction, a concept he found dubious, tracing its roots in Enlightenment philosophy to Max Weber, whom he described as a "serious and noble mind" but who, in Strauss's view, was deeply influenced by Nietzsche's relativism. For Strauss, politics could not be studied from afar; a political scientist using a value-free scientific eye was self-deluded. Positivism, as the heir to Auguste Comte and Weber, failed to justify its own existence, which requires a value judgment. While modern liberalism emphasized individual liberty, Strauss advocated greater attention to human excellence and political virtue, constantly raising the question of how freedom and excellence can coexist without providing a straightforward answer to the Socratic question: What is the good for the city and man? Two significant political-philosophical dialogues Strauss had with living thinkers were with Carl Schmitt and Alexandre Kojève. Schmitt, who later became chief jurist of Nazi Germany, was one of the first important German academics to positively review Strauss's early work, particularly on Hobbes, and his approval was instrumental in securing Strauss the scholarship that allowed him to leave Germany. According to Heinrich Meier's interpretation, Strauss's critique of Schmitt's The Concept of the Political led Schmitt to make significant emendations in its second edition. In a 1932 letter to Schmitt, Strauss summarized Schmitt's political theology as stating that because man is by nature evil, he needs dominion, which can be established only through unity against other men; every association of men is necessarily a separation from others, and thus the political, as understood, is not the constitutive principle of the state.

Freedom and excellence can coexist, according to Leo Strauss, who refused to offer a direct answer to the Socratic question of what is good for the city and man. Strauss engaged in two significant political-philosophical dialogues with living thinkers: Carl Schmitt and Alexandre Kojève. Schmitt, who later served as chief jurist of Nazi Germany, was one of the first prominent German academics to positively review Strauss’s early work, particularly his interpretation of Hobbes, and this endorsement helped secure Strauss the scholarship that enabled him to leave Germany. According to Heinrich Meier, Strauss’s critique of Schmitt’s *The Concept of the Political* prompted Schmitt to make substantial revisions in its second edition. In a 1932 letter, Strauss summarized Schmitt’s political theology as asserting that because man is by nature evil, dominion is necessary, and unity can only be achieved through a unity against others; every association is a separation from others, so the political is not the foundation of the state but a condition of it. Robert Howse, however, claims there is no clear evidence for this influence, suggesting the relationship was merely professional. Strauss directly opposed Schmitt, viewing Schmitt’s return to Hobbes as clarifying the nature of political existence and modern self-understanding, but arguing that Schmitt’s transformation of political thought into a political theology was inadequate. Strauss instead advocated a return to a broader classical understanding of human nature and a revival of ancient political philosophy. With Kojève, Strauss maintained a close and lifelong philosophical friendship, first meeting as students in Berlin; Kojève later stated that without befriending Strauss, he never would have known what philosophy is. Their central dispute centered on the role of philosophy in politics: Kojève, a senior civil servant instrumental in founding the European Economic Community, believed philosophers should actively shape political events, while Strauss maintained that philosophers should only participate in politics to the extent that philosophy remains free from political interference. Strauss argued that modern liberalism, oriented toward universal freedom rather than ancient liberalism focused on human excellence, contains an inherent tendency toward extreme relativism, leading to two forms of nihilism. Believing that 20th-century relativism, scientism, historicism, and nihilism contributed to the decline of modern society and philosophy, Strauss sought to trace these philosophical pathways and advocated a return to classical political philosophy as a basis for evaluating political action. He argued that Plato’s *Republic* is not a blueprint for regime reform (a reference to Karl Popper’s critique), but rather reveals the nature of political things—the nature of the city. Strauss claimed the city-in-speech is unnatural because it arises from the abstraction from eros. Though skeptical of progress, he was equally skeptical of political agendas of "return," fearing that attempting to resolve debates between rationalism and traditionalism would be dangerous. He expressed concern about efforts to establish a world state, fearing such a structure would inevitably become a tyranny, and thus remained distant from both fascism and communism. Strauss rejected Karl Popper’s views as illogical; in response to Eric Voegelin’s letter criticizing Popper’s understanding of Plato, Voegelin stated that Popper was philosophically uncultured and incapable of correctly understanding even a single page of Plato, calling the study a waste of time and an annoyance. Strauss shared this letter with Kurt Riezler, who used his influence to oppose Popper’s appointment at the University of Chicago. Strauss consistently emphasized two key dichotomies in political philosophy: Athens and Jerusalem (reason and revelation) and Ancient versus Modern. The "Ancients" include the Socratic philosophers and their heirs; the "Moderns" begin with Niccolò Machiavelli. The contrast reflects the unresolved tension between reason and revelation. The Socratics, reacting to early Greek philosophers, brought philosophy back to earth and to the political sphere. The Moderns, reacting to the dominance of revelation in medieval society, promoted reason, rejecting Aquinas’s fusion of natural right and natural theology, which they saw as vulnerable to theological disputes. Thomas Hobbes, influenced by Francis Bacon, shifted political thought toward human physical fears and hopes, setting a precedent for John Locke, David Hume, and Adam Smith. As a youth, Strauss was part of the German Zionist youth group with Gershom Scholem and Walter Benjamin, both of whom remained admirers throughout their lives. At age 17, Strauss was "converted" to political Zionism under Ze'ev Jabotinsky, writing essays on its controversies before abandoning the activities by his early twenties. While maintaining a sympathetic interest in Zionism, he later regarded it as "problematic" and became disillusioned with some of its goals. Strauss taught at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem during the 1954–55 academic year. In a letter to a *National Review* editor, he questioned why Israel had been labeled a racist state, arguing the author lacked sufficient proof, and concluded that political Zionism is problematic for obvious reasons, yet it served as a vital moral force in an era of dissolution by resisting the leveling of ancestral differences and fulfilling a conservative function. Strauss accepted the utility of religious belief but was openly disdainful of atheism and disapproved of contemporary "dogmatic disbelief," which he considered irrational. Like Thomas Aquinas, he believed revelation must be subject to rational examination. In *The City and Man*, he invites readers to consider "what is God?" (p. 241), and Edward Feser notes that Strauss was neither an orthodox believer nor a convinced atheist, maintaining that orthodoxy remains a defensible option alongside unbelief. In *Natural Right and History*, Strauss distinguishes a Socratic (Platonic, Ciceronian, Aristotelian) from a conventionalist (materialistic, Epicurean) reading of divinity, arguing that the question of religion is inseparable from the nature of civil society and authority. He defends the Socratic reading and rejects the conventionalist one, which includes atheism. This view contradicts interpretations by Shadia Drury and others who claim Strauss viewed religion instrumentally. Strauss’s works were admired by thinkers such as Gershom Scholem, Walter Benjamin, Hans-Georg Gadamer, Alexandre Kojève, and Jacques Lacan. Benjamin, who met Strauss as a student in Berlin, expressed lifelong admiration. Gadamer stated he largely agreed with Strauss’s interpretations. "Straussianism" refers to the research methods, concepts, presuppositions, central questions, and pedagogical style characteristic of many conservatives influenced by Strauss. It is especially influential among university professors of historical political theory and also serves as a common intellectual framework among conservative activists, think tank professionals, and public intellectuals. Harvey Mansfield, Steven B. Smith, and Steven Berg, though not students of Strauss, are considered Straussians. Mansfield argues there is no such thing as "Straussianism" but rather Straussians and a school of Straussians, describing the school as open to all of philosophy without requiring specific beliefs. Within political theory, the Straussian method involves a "close reading" of the "Great Books," aiming to understand a thinker as he understood himself, without concern for historical context or influence, and with an openness to finding timeless truths. Great books are seen as authored by thinkers of sovereign critical self-knowledge and intellectual power, beyond the reach of their historical context, while lesser works are considered epiphenomenal. This approach counters mid-20th-century historicism, which views political thought as progressing linearly, and suggests that past thinkers may hold truths that contemporary thinkers have missed. Almost all of Strauss’s writings have been translated into Chinese, with a notable school of Chinese Straussians, including Liu Xiaofeng and Gan Yang. "Chinese Straussians," often also interested in Carl Schmitt, exemplify the adaptation of Western political theory in non-Western contexts. As editors of a recent volume note, the reception of Schmitt and Strauss in the Chinese-speaking world reveals insights into Western modernity’s contradictions and non-liberal societies’ dilemmas. Critics have accused Strauss of being elitist, illiberal, and anti-democratic. Seymour Hersh has claimed Strauss endorsed "noble lies," myths used by leaders to maintain social cohesion. In *The City and Man*, Strauss discusses Plato’s Republic myths, including the belief that state land belongs to the state even if acquired illegitimately and that citizenship is based on more than birth. Shadia Drury, in *Leo Strauss and the American Right*, claims Strauss instilled an elitist strain in American political leaders linked to imperialist militarism, neoconservatism, and Christian fundamentalism, arguing that Strauss taught that perpetual deception of citizens by rulers is necessary because they need strong leaders to guide them. Some conservatives, like Claes G. Ryn, criticize Strauss for creating an artificial contrast between moral universality and the conventional, ancestral, and historical. Ryn argues Strauss wrongly assumes that respect for tradition undermines reason and universality, and that genuine universality is known in concretized, particular forms. He contends that Strauss’s abstract, ahistorical conception of natural right distorts true universality and that his views have led American conservatives—especially Catholic intellectuals—to reject tradition in favor of ahistorical theorizing, contrary to the Christian notion of the Incarnation, which unites the universal and historical. Ryn sees Strauss’s anti-historicism as connected to the French Jacobins, who also viewed tradition as incompatible with virtue and rationality. Paul Gottfried describes the "new Jacobinism" of neoconservatism as echoing the rhetoric of Louis Antoine de Saint-Just and Leon Trotsky, adopted by the philosophically unprepared American Right. In *Straussophobia*, Peter Minowitz offers a detailed critique of Drury, Xenos, and others, accusing them of bigotry and buffoonery. Steven B. Smith, in *Reading Leo Strauss*, rejects the link between Strauss and neoconservatism, asserting that Strauss was never politically active, never supported imperialism, and questioned the usefulness of political philosophy in shaping policy. He argues that Plato’s myth of the philosopher king should be read as a reductio ad absurdum, and that philosophers should engage politics only to preserve philosophy’s autonomy. Robert Alter, in reviewing Smith’s work, finds Smith’s argument persuasive in correcting misconceptions about Strauss’s political views. Strauss’s daughter, Jenny Strauss Clay, defended him against accusations of being the mastermind behind neoconservative foreign policy, stating he was a conservative in opposing the idea that change is always progress. Since contemporary academia leaned left with its faith in progress and science and discomfort with moral judgment, Strauss stood outside the academic consensus. If academia had leaned right, he would have questioned it too—on certain occasions he did. Mark Lilla argues that attributing neoconservative views to Strauss contradicts a careful reading of his texts, especially *On Tyranny*, summarizing Strauss as emphasizing the need for philosophy to recognize tyranny’s dangers and to defend its autonomy without believing it can shape politics. Responding to claims that Strauss’s teachings led to George W. Bush-era foreign policy, such as spreading liberal democracy through military force, Nathan Tarcov, director of the Leo Strauss Center at the University of Chicago, asserts that Strauss was essentially non-political. After analyzing the limited practical political views in Strauss’s writings, Tarcov concludes that Strauss reminds us of enduring political problems, but we are solely responsible for our flawed solutions. Books and articles on Maimonides and Jewish philosophy are also part of Strauss’s body of work.
Today, there are writings about Maimonides and Jewish philosophy, including books and articles.
